title: The outcaste at Kashi
hook: a great teacher tells a man to step aside, and Shiva answers with a question
carry: shiva lives in everyone, so everyone gets the bow

segments.voice: Yesterday: namah, the bow leaves no one out, the Rudram's heartbeat, said again and again.
screen: `NAMAH — A BOW.` · `TODAY: WHO GETS THE BOW.`

segments.voice: Kashi, on the banks of the Ganga, early morning. The young teacher Shankara is walking up from his bath with his students when a man blocks the narrow lane, a man the town treated as an outcaste, with four dogs at his heels. The students call out: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead. Which should step aside? This body from your body, both made of the same food? Or the Self in me from the Self in you, when it's the same Self? Shankara stops.
screen: `KASHI. A NARROW LANE.` → `MOVE ASIDE.` → `WHICH ONE OF ME SHOULD MOVE?`

segments.voice: Tradition says Shankara bowed to the man right there, and that the outcaste was Shiva himself, with the four Vedas as his dogs. The short poem Shankara is said to have made that morning, the Manisha Panchakam, says it plainly: whoever sees the one Self in all, brahmin or outcaste, is my teacher. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the same Lord lives in every being. The Rudram sings it in its own way. In one stretch of the Namakam, the bows come in pairs. A bow to the short one, and to the dwarf. To the large one, and to the one grown old. To the eldest, and to the youngest. To the firstborn, and to the one born after. To the middle one, and to the one not yet grown, still unsure of themselves. Rudra is all of them. Short and tall, first and last: the very measures people use to rank each other. The hymn doesn't erase the differences. It names every one, and gives every one the same small word, namah. Nobody's bow is louder. Many teachers read the folded hands of namaste the same way: a bow to the divine in the person in front of you. In a Hindu home, children still touch their elders' feet, and that respect is real. But the bow itself, in the Rudram, goes to every rung, down to the shy kid at the end of the table.
screen: `SHIVA, AS THE OUTCASTE.` · `THE SAME LORD IN EVERY BEING.` · `THE ELDEST, THE YOUNGEST, THE SHY ONE.` · `THE SAME BOW FOR EVERY RUNG.` · then, large: `NOBODY'S NAMAH IS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people in your family, or the family you've made, from the eldest you can think of down to the youngest, and give each one a breath and the same inward bow, hands folded at the heart if you like, the way you'd say namaste. If one is harder to bow to, stay a little longer with that one. If you pray, you can say namah shivaya for each of them; if you don't, the quiet bow is enough.
The Rudram. Today's lines: a bow to the eldest and the youngest, the firstborn and the later-born, the middle one and the shy one. And the outcaste in the lane at Kashi, who was Shiva.
Your line: Shiva lives in everyone, so everyone gets the bow. Even the one you'd ask to step aside. Go gently.

howItsDone: Chanters learn the Namakam's paired lines (namo jyeshthaya cha kanishthaya cha and others) by heart, usually from a teacher, and recite them in Vedic Sanskrit at home, in temples and in group chanting.

Namakam.meaning: the Rudram's first part, built on namah, a bow

namah.meaning: a bow, homage, a gesture of honor

Rudra.meaning: a Vedic name; tradition knows Rudra and Shiva as one

Rudram.meaning: a hymn to Rudra in the Krishna Yajur Veda

Shankara.meaning: Adi Shankara, a great early teacher of Vedanta

sources.ref: Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.5–4.5.6 (Shri Rudram, Namakam: the short and the dwarf, the large and the old, the eldest and the youngest, the firstborn and the later-born, the middle one and the immature)
Manisha Panchakam (attributed to Adi Shankara; traditionally set at Kashi after the meeting with the chandala: whoever sees the one Self in all is my teacher)
Shankara Digvijaya attributed to Madhava-Vidyaranya (the chandala at Kashi revealed as Shiva, the four dogs as the four Vedas)
